passages.where: A psalm that has prayed against being forsaken ends in certainty that the psalmist will see God's goodness in the land of the living, and with a call to wait for the LORD. The site's plain note says the psalm ends before the answer comes, and that wait patiently for the LORD is said twice, because once is rarely enough.

From the depths the psalmist waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning, and says it twice. The site's plain note says the psalm does not promise when the morning comes, only that it will, because God's love keeps its word, and that the man who prayed it was still waiting when it ended.

In a book of ruin, a man who has felt God's hand against him calls to mind God's mercies and says it is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD. The site's note says the chapter lives inside the tension without solving it, and that its hope is chosen rather than felt.

Habakkuk takes his stand on the watchtower to see what God will answer, and is told to write the vision plainly, because it awaits its appointed time. Though it lingers, he is to wait for it, since it will surely come. The next verse says the righteous will live by faith.

After years of waiting, Sarah bears Isaac at the very time God had promised. The site's note says the verse repeats God's faithfulness twice so that no reader can miss it, and its plain note says God kept a promise that took twenty-five years. It also adds a word of care: Sarah's story does not promise a child to every couple who prays for one, and childlessness is not a judgment from God.

John says Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus, and in the same breath that when he heard Lazarus was sick he stayed where he was for two days. The site's note says John asks the reader to read the delay by the love, and that the verse does not explain every delay but rules out the conclusion that waiting means indifference. Its plain note says being loved by Jesus and facing a long, frightening wait can both be true at once.

James tells suffering believers to be patient like a farmer who waits for the rains, and to strengthen their hearts. The site's plain note says James does not promise that patient people will always be put right in this life, and that be patient is never a word to someone being abused or exploited that they must stay and bear it.

An old man counsels the faithful to be still before the LORD and wait patiently, and not to fret when others prosper by wrong. The site's plain note says stillness is not doing nothing; it is refusing to be pushed by envy.

Paul says that believers were saved in hope, and that hope by its nature looks for what is not yet seen. The site's note says Christian hope is certain in its object and unseen in its present experience, and is lived not as anxiety but as patient endurance.

The risen Jesus tells his followers not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the gift the Father promised. When they ask about dates, the site's plain note says, he gives them a job instead, and promises that power will come to them for a task too big for them.

whole: Waiting has many faces: a diagnosis with no answer yet, years of trying for a child, a son or daughter who has not come home, a job search that will not end, a marriage that has not healed, a prayer prayed so long that the words have worn smooth. Some waiting is for something good that has not come; some is for something hard to be over. Either way the days go slowly, other people's lives seem to move on, and it is easy to start hearing God's silence as a no, or as not caring at all.

Scripture knows how long God's people have had to wait. Abraham and Sarah waited twenty-five years for the son God promised, and the site's note says the birth came at the very time God had set. The disciples were told to wait in Jerusalem without being told for how long. Psalm 27 tells the reader to wait twice, because once is rarely enough. And when Jesus heard that Lazarus was sick, John says he loved the family and stayed where he was for two days; the note on that verse says it does not explain every delay, but it rules out the conclusion that waiting means indifference. The hard thing about waiting is not only the time. It is what the time seems to say.

So the wisdom of Scripture is not a technique for shortening the wait but a way to wait. Keep bringing the request honestly, as the widow in Jesus' parable kept coming back. Be still rather than fretting at people whose lives seem to move faster. Wait like a farmer, strengthening your heart rather than grumbling. Do the plain work in front of you, as the disciples were given a job instead of a date. Tell the truth about how hard it is, and lean on people who have waited longer than you. And hear the limit the site's note on James 5 sets: patience is never a word to someone being abused or exploited that they must stay and bear it.

The hope Scripture gives is not that every wait ends the way we hope; the same note says many of the prophets were not rescued in this life. It is that the one we wait for is good, and that hope by its nature looks for what is not yet seen. In the middle of ruin, Lamentations says it is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD, and Habakkuk was told the vision would surely come, though it lingered. The God who seems slow is not absent, and the waiting is not wasted on him.
sit: What are you waiting for that you have stopped telling God about, and what is one thing in front of you that you could do faithfully while you wait?

prayer.lead: The psalm closes with a whole congregation waiting together. The site's plain note asks what you hope in, since none of the things people trust can save; pray these lines with others, or for them.

careLines.text: Waiting is not a failure of faith.
Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
